research_question: Why does plastic waste persist in the environment, and how does it fragment into microplastics?

sources.title: Everything you need to know about plastic pollution
notes: Most common plastics do not biodegrade like organic matter; they fragment over time.
Plastic waste can persist in ecosystems and affect soil, water and wildlife.
Reducing waste and keeping materials in circulation are central prevention approaches.

sources.title: Can marine debris degrade on its own in the environment?
notes: Degradation time depends on material, size, thickness and environmental conditions.
Photodegradable plastics can break into microplastics rather than fully disappear.
Scientists continue investigating the impacts of microplastics on marine life.

sources.title: Biodegradable Plastics Are Not the Answer to Reducing Marine Litter, Says UN
notes: Some plastics marketed as biodegradable need industrial conditions rarely met in marine environments.
Fragmentation into microplastics is not the same as complete biodegradation.
Labels should not be assumed to mean a product will safely disappear in nature.

sources.title: Plastics in the environment in the context of UV radiation, climate change and the Montreal Protocol: UNEP Environmental Effects Assessment Panel, Update 2023
sources.reliability: Scientific assessment report hosted by NOAA
notes: Sunlight and weathering can reduce plastic durability and create micro- and nanoplastic particles.
Plastic debris persists in soils, water bodies and the atmosphere.
Potential biological risks remain an active area of research.

sources.title: Pollution to Solution: Accessing marine litter and plastic pollution
notes: Plastic fragments into smaller particles rather than biodegrading like organic matter.
Plastic fragments and nanoplastics can spread through water and ecosystems.
Prevention and improved waste systems address pollution before fragments become difficult to remove.
